newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ lobby urges capital gains tax review.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ lobby urges capital gains tax review.

text.p: The head of New Zealand's Investment Savings and Insurance Association (ISI) said on Tuesday it would press the next government for a review of capital gains taxation, especially on passive investment funds.

Chief Executive Roger Gill also said he expected a tax ruling by the British-based Privy Council in favour of Wellington company Rangatira Ltd would do little to clarify the murky dividing line between traders and non-traders of shares.
He said the conservative National Party, now running a caretaker government, had shied from a review of taxation of investment gains.

Gill said the ISI wanted official recognition that a de facto capital gains tax regime existed. A whole rash of index-hugging funds had cropped up because their gains were assessed as not subject to taxation, he said.

"The government of the day has been saying there is no capital gains regime in New Zealand and they don't want to start a capital gains tax, but the fact remains that there is...a very lumpy sort of regime. We lurch from court case to court case."

Gill said Tuesday's news that the Privy Council had ruled in favour of Rangatira would do little to dispel the uncertainty. It ruled against the Inland Revenue Department (IRD), which argued that Rangatira had acted as a share trader and should therefore pay back taxes of NZ$3.8 million.
"The judgment itself is probably limited to a certain set of facts, and in terms of principle the case probably hasn't taken the debate very much further at all," Gill said.

"I think it just underlines the importance of getting some clarity there so we don't have to resort to going to the Court of Appeal or the Privy Council every time we've got an assessment problem with the IRD. Our preference would be for some sort of benchmark beyond which you became a trader, rather than leaving it to the individual to decide and then for the IRD to assess."
Gill said the indexed funds, which seek to replicate at low cost the performance of market averages, were purely tax-driven.

Through them, investors avoid the capital gains tax incurred with unit trusts, insurance bonds and registered superannuation schemes. The New Zealand Stock Exchange set the ball rolling in June with the launch of its TeNZ fund, which tracks the exchange's NZSE-10 index. Since then around five more passive funds have been announced, tracking a range of indices.
"I guess the challenge is on the active manager to beat the index and to provide the returns," Gill said.
He said the IFA wrote to all political parties before the election seeking their commitment to a post-election review of capital gains taxation.
"I think the responses were fairly predictable. The government couldn't see anything new...two or three other parties thought it would be a good idea, and New Zealand First didn't reply at all.

"What we've got to do is provide the evidence to whoever the new government is, to make the case, and then to at least try and encourage the government to review the situation. Whether anything will come of it will remain to be seen."
"Experience has shown it can be quite a drawn-out process. The development of the unit trust taxation regime took place over about three years," Gill said.
The New Zealand First Party holds the balance of power after the election, and is currently negotiating with both National and centre-left Labour over the shape of the new government.

Members of the Life Office Association (LOA) and the Investment Funds Association (IFA) combined in August to form the ISI, representing insurance and investment products, to win more lobbying clout. It represents more than NZ$8 billion of investment funds and 600,000 investors and policy holders.
